title: VALUExBRK 2026 | Bill Ackman, Mohnish Pabrai, Tom Gayner, Chris Bloomstran & More
description:
Join Guy Spier and an extraordinary lineup of investors, entrepreneurs, fund managers, and thinkers at VALUExBRK 2026 in Omaha. This year's event featured wide-ranging discussions on investing, Berkshire Hathaway, AI, business quality, capital allocation, permanent capital, entrepreneurship, and life lessons from decades in markets and business.

Chapters:
Guy Spier — Welcome and Winning Points Against the Grim Reaper Opening remarks on storytelling, joy, and lessons from a difficult year — including reflections on the February letter and the GBM diagnosis.

Steven Myhill-Jones — How Charlie Munger Recruited Me to Daily Journal 
The Daily Journal CEO on the lunch in LA, the phone call that began with "before you say no, I'm almost 98," and why public-sector complexity is a moat in the age of AI.

Adam Mead — 60 Years of Berkshire by the Numbers 
The author of The Complete Financial History of Berkshire Hathaway on the data: more equity capital added in the last 5 years than in Berkshire's first 52, and the pivotal Gen Re deal at 3x book.

Bryan Lawrence — Meet Marvin and Vicki, Our AI Agents at Oakcliff 
Two AI agents running on Mac minis. Bryan's takeaway: businesses with revenues denominated in human time but costs in tokens face a structural problem.

Bill Ackman — Creativity, Permanent Capital, and Howard Hughes 
Why creativity in investing means doing things that haven't been done before, and how Howard Hughes is being built into a "mini-Berkshire."

Tom Gayner — Choosing Your Game, and Why I Read War and Peace Aloud 
The Markel CEO on knowing your edge ("I'm not racing Usain Bolt") a
summary: The interview argues that while companies selling compute like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft trade at high valuations, investors should look for opportunities where short-term AI-driven insights create buying chances in other sectors. Specifically, the speaker highlights Fairfax Financial as a compelling opportunity similar to Berkshire Hathaway 30 years ago, citing its strong compounding history, decentralized structure, and current metrics. The thesis suggests that Fairfax has resolved legacy issues and is now delivering consistent profits with a clear path to growth, positioning it in a 'sweet spot' for compounding.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Fairfax Financial as a compelling investment opportunity similar to Berkshire Hathaway 30 years ago, citing its strong compounding history, decentralized structure, and current metrics.
claims.quote: So I'm going to talk about Fairfax Financial and I'm going to frame this conversation entirely through a lens that resonates or should resonate with everybody in the room. what Bergkshire Hathaway looked like 30 years ago before size became its greatest constraint. So Fairfax was built on a similar blueprint.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Fairfax has delivered an 18.6% compound annual growth rate since 2017 with a growing float and a large investment portfolio generating significant returns.
claims.quote: Since 2017, Fairfax has delivered an 18.6 compound annual growth rate with float growing at 18%, a 74.9 billion investment portfolio, and a greater than 5 billion annual operating income rate.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Since inception, Fairfax's book value per share has compounded at 18.7% annually, and its share price has outperformed the S&P 500, ranking it in the top 1% of US-listed companies since 1985.
claims.quote: Since inception in 1985, book value per share has compounded at 18.7% annually against its stated target of 15% over the long term. Share price in USD has compounded at 19.5% versus 11.5% for the S&P 500.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Fairfax operates through a highly decentralized model with empowered managers, long tenures, and deep ownership cultures, building businesses to compound rather than optimizing for the next quarter.
claims.quote: Like Bergkshire, Fairfax operates through a highly decentralized model. Subsidiaries run are run by empowered managers with long tenures and deep ownership cultures. This is not a bureaucracy optimizing for the next quarter.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Fairfax has resolved legacy hedging positions and is now delivering consistent underwriting profits and investment returns, with a clear path to significant annual operating income.
claims.quote: Since 2017, Fairfax has found its stride resolving the legacy hedging positions that weighed on returns from 2010 to 2016. repositioning the investment portfolio and delivering a 18.6 compounded annual growth rate over eight years.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Fairfax's recent performance includes strong underwriting profits, high investment returns, and significant growth in float, with management setting explicit forward earnings targets.
claims.quote: gross premiums written of 33.3 billion, a 93% combined ratio producing $1.8 billion dollars of underwriting profit consistent even through a catastrophe year. And I will note in these numbers there's $1.2 billion of catastroph catastrophe losses embedded in those numbers.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: Fairfax's shareholders equity and market cap are comparable to Berkshire Hathaway at specific milestones, suggesting Fairfax is in the sweet spot of compounding and still has room to grow.
claims.quote: Fairfax's shareholders equity of 26 billion. Berkshire was there in 1997. Bloat of 40.8 billion. Bergkshire crossed that in 2002. An investment portfolio of 74.9 billion. Berkshire hit that mark in 2002.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: The speaker compares Fairfax's metrics to Berkshire Hathaway's historical milestones, noting that Berkshire's size now constrains its ability to make moves that meaningfully change outcomes for shareholders.
claims.quote: what Bergkshire Hathaway looked like 30 years ago before size became its greatest constraint. So Fairfax was built on a similar blueprint. insurance float as permanent capital, value investing on the asset side, founder control, and a decentralized structure that trusts managers and essentially leaves them alone.
claims.speaker: Lauren

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that his father dresses out of Walmart and that Costco would be an expensive purchase for him, illustrating his classic value investor style.
claims.quote: My dad is a true value investor. He dresses out of Walmart. He um you know Costco would be an expensive purchase for him. He just showed up for his meeting with his estate attorney with all of his documents in a Walmart plastic bag that had been recycled.
claims.speaker: Lauren
